item.title: Configuring Dependency Injection in JAX-RS with Jersey and HK2
item.description:
“Configuring Dependency Injection in JAX-RS with Jersey and HK2”

When building RESTful services using JAX-RS (like Jersey), providing services and managing component lifecycles is crucial. How does one effectively integrate dependency injection (DI) mechanisms, such as HK2 or CDI, to facilitate the injection of services into JAX-RS resources? Various strategies exist, ranging from explicit binding to leveraging container features.

Primary Approach: Defining and Registering an AbstractBinder

The foundational method involves explicitly defining how your dependencies should be instantiated and registered within your JAX-RS application configuration. This utilizes Jersey’s built-in HK2 binding mechanism.

item.title: Implementing Token Authentication and Authorization in JAX-RS 2 0
item.description:
“Implementing Token Authentication and Authorization in JAX-RS 2 0”

Token-based authentication presents an alternative to traditional session management. At its core, a client swaps persistent credentials (like username and password) for a temporary data artifact—the token. Subsequent requests leverage this token for verification instead of repeatedly sending the initial credentials.

How does this sequence operate in practice?

  1. Credential Submission: The client transmits user credentials (username/password) to the server.
  2. Token Generation: Upon validating these credentials, the server produces a unique token intended for the user.
  3. Server Storage: The server records this newly generated token, associating it with the user ID and setting an expiration time in persistent storage.
  4. Token Return: The server sends the created token back to the client.
  5. Subsequent Requests: The client includes this token with every following request directed to the server.
  6. Token Verification: For each incoming request, the server extracts the token, looks up associated user details to confirm authenticity.

If the token verification succeeds, the server processes the request. Failure results in a request denial. Following successful authentication, the server then proceeds to authorization checks. Some token schemes feature an explicit endpoint for token refreshment.

item.title: Servlet Context getRealPath: Best Practices and Alternatives for Resource Access
item.description:
“Servlet Context getRealPath: Best Practices and Alternatives for Resource Access”

The ServletContext#getRealPath(String path) method serves a specific purpose: translating a virtual path within the deployed web application structure (often residing inside an expanded WAR folder on the server’s disk) into an absolute file system path. The path specified starts relative to the web content root, which is conventionally represented by /.

For a typical project layout:

YourWebProject
 |-- src
 |    :
 |
 |-- web
 |    |-- META-INF
 |    |    `-- MANIFEST.MF
 |    |-- WEB-INF
 |    |    `-- web.xml
 |    |-- index.jsp
 |    `-- login.jsp
 :

Passing / to getRealPath() yields the absolute disk location corresponding to the /web directory of the expanded WAR archive, for example, /path/to/server/work/folder/some.war/.

item.title: Fix javax servlet http HttpServlet Not Found in Eclipse
item.description:
“Fix javax servlet http HttpServlet Not Found in Eclipse”

Encountering the “The superclass ‘javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet’ was not found on the Java Build Path” error in Eclipse can be a common hurdle when developing Java web applications. This typically arises when your project’s build path is not correctly configured to include the necessary Servlet API libraries provided by your application server. Let’s explore the various reasons and solutions for this pervasive issue.
